title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Ypsilanti weighs a year-long data center halt as protests hit a closed West Michigan seminar.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy, the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're digging into closed-door meetings, resident protests, and new local pushback on data centers from Allegan County to Ypsilanti.
Graham, the lead story today is that invite-only seminar in Dorr Township where more than 100 officials from Allegan, Barry and Kent counties gathered while dozens protested outside.
Exactly. The session focused on zoning and inspections and was hosted by a private firm. Residents raised concerns about water use and a Microsoft proposal that remains under moratorium until 2027.
Why does a closed meeting like this matter so much to people living 30 miles away?
Because any new facilities could affect electric bills and water supplies across a wide region. Demonstrators outside highlighted how these projects strain resources that everyone shares.
What's the history here? Has Michigan seen this kind of pushback before?

Yes, several communities have already paused or tightened rules on standalone data centers. Ypsilanti is debating a year-long halt tonight, and places like Wixom have advanced new restrictions despite lawsuit threats from developers.
Who are the main players in these deals?

You have the data center developers pitching projects, municipal leaders handling zoning, and residents worried about farmland loss, higher utility rates, and traffic. State law also lets firms keep tax break details private.
How does this connect to electric bills specifically?

New facilities draw massive power. Vice-presidential candidate Vance highlighted this at his Sterling Heights stop yesterday, linking data center growth to potential rate hikes and tying it to University of Michigan research.
What about water? That seems to come up everywhere.

Cooling these centers requires huge amounts of water. In Dorr, protesters flagged that risk alongside the Microsoft proposal. Similar worries appear in Saline Township with The Barn project and near Ann Arbor at the million-hour construction milestone.
Farmland is another big piece, right?

Absolutely. The Barn is rising fast on farmland in Saline Township, and residents there are already seeing new power lines and traffic changes. Washtenaw County communities are tracking how quickly land use shifts.
What happens next after a meeting like the one in Dorr?
Local officials will likely refine zoning rules. Ypsilanti's council meets tonight to consider that temporary ban, which would buy time for permanent regulations before any large projects arrive.
Is there precedent for these moratoriums working?
Several townships have used them to study impacts. Wixom tightened rules recently even with legal threats looming, and Madison Heights just received its first site plan filing on Sunday.
How transparent are these processes for regular residents?

That's a sticking point. The closed-door format in Dorr left many wondering whose voices shape the deals. State law allowing hidden tax incentives adds to the opacity, potentially shifting costs to local taxpayers.
What about the grid and roads in places like Lyon Township?
A developer there faces another hearing next month. Residents have already flagged power demand and local impacts from the project.
Any sense of how many communities are watching this right now?
Quite a few. From Oakland County suburbs to West Michigan, officials and residents are tracking proposals that could affect bills and services even 30 miles away.
So the bigger picture is communities trying to get ahead of rapid buildout?
That's the core tension. Economic opportunities versus long-term costs to utilities, water, and land use.
Graham, let's move to quick hits. Ypsilanti is debating that year-long halt tonight—what exactly is on the table?

City leaders will discuss a temporary ban on new standalone data center proposals. Residents fear spikes in electricity rates and water strain, and the moratorium would allow time for permanent zoning rules.
Vance spoke in Sterling Heights yesterday about this. What did he say?
He framed data center growth as both an economic opportunity and a risk to utility costs, linking it to University of Michigan research and trucking impacts for Michigan voters.
Another closed-door pitch drew protests yesterday too.
Officials from across the region heard pitches while demonstrators rallied outside. Residents 30 miles away could face higher bills and water strain if those projects advance.
On the construction side, that Ann Arbor-area facility hit a million hours yesterday.
Washtenaw County residents are watching power rates and water use as it ramps up. Local jobs are growing, but questions about long-term taxpayer costs remain.
Saline Township's The Barn project is moving fast.
Construction is advancing rapidly on farmland there. Nearby residents will see new power lines, traffic, and potential tax shifts once it's online.
Michigan law lets data centers hide tax breaks.
That's right. It reduces transparency on revenue losses for cities and townships, which can mean higher local taxes or strained services elsewhere.
Madison Heights got its first site plan filing on Sunday.
It's the first concrete step in that Oakland County suburb. Effects could ripple to residents 30 miles away through power and water strain.
Wixom tightened rules despite lawsuit threats.
Officials advanced new restrictions on large projects that would draw heavy power and water. Changes could affect local taxes, traffic, and rates.
Lyon Township has that hearing coming up next month.
Residents there continue raising concerns over grid and road impacts from the proposed project.
Now for on deck. What's happening tonight that listeners can attend?
Ypsilanti city council meets tonight to debate that year-long data center moratorium. It's open to the public and directly addresses the rate and water concerns we've been discussing.
Any other meetings worth noting?
Lyon Township planners will hear from the data center developer again next month. Check local agendas for exact dates and times.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Closed Doors in Dorr Spark Fears Over Power, Water and Farmland
